Complex minds can't develop on their own. [...] For a mind to even approach its full potential, it needs cultivation by other minds.”
—Ted Chiang, The Lifecycle of Software Objects (2010)
1 Introduction
extend the framework of Major Evolutionary Transitions (METs) to human–AI relations. B0y comparing increasingly tight human–AI coupling with canonical transitions such as chromosomes, eukaryotic cells, and multicellularity, they ask whether cooperation, division of labor, and aligned interests could eventually produce a new evolutionary individual. This is a productive question because it relocates discussion from isolated machine capability to organization across scales (
). The present article does not replace that framework or criticize it for failing to answer a different question. It offers a supplement: even if a human–AI composite acquired some properties of an evolutionary individual, what additional organization would make it a cognitive individual?
Individuality has no single accepted currency. Biological and philosophical accounts emphasize, among other things, reproduction and selection, operational closure, autonomy, informational integration, temporal persistence, and organism–environment partitioning (
;
;
;
). These criteria are relevant to human–AI composites. Yet none by itself determines whether heterogeneous information is organized into contents that can guide perception, action, inference, and evaluation across time. I therefore treat representational architecture as a domain-specific criterion of cognitive—not biological—individuality. It is privileged here because the target phenomenon is meaningful, flexible cognition: the capacity to preserve referential relations, recombine event content, compare alternatives, and revise commitments.
